div.p: To you, blessed one, I sing, the earth's renowned support, the much-loved light of the warlike sons of Aeneas, sweet scion of Ausonian Zeus, Antoninus; whom great Domna bore to great Severus, bedded in blessedness and in blessedness brought to birth, a bride of the noblest husband, a mother of fairest children, an Assyrian Cytherea and a Selene that never wanes, in no way feebler than the offspring of Zeus the son of Cronus; may Titan Phaethon and Phoebus Apollo look upon you with favour. To him the father, toiling with his mighty hands, gave to hold all the dry land and all the watery deep. For you the teeming all-bountiful soil conceives and bears, and again the sea in calm weather feeds its famous tribes; for you all the streams flow down from Ocean, and the bright glad Dawn, the early-born, runs on her course. Therefore I long to sing the glorious lore of the hunt. This Calliope bids me, this Artemis herself. I heard, as is right, I heard the divine voice, and I answered the goddess; and first she spoke to me thus: A. Awake, and let us tread the rugged path that no mortal yet has trodden in his songs. O. Be gracious, holy lady, and what you purpose in your heart, I will utter in our mortal human voice. A. I do not wish you now to sing of the triennial mountain-Bacchus, nor of the dance beside the deeps of Aonian Asopus. O. I will leave, as you command, the nightly Sabazian rites; often I have danced the round for Thyonean Dionysus. A. Do not speak of the race of heroes, nor of seafaring Argo, nor of the battles of men, nor sing to me of the Slayer of Mortals. O. I will not tell of wars, nor of the most wretched works of Ares; I have set my mind on the woes of the Parthians and on Ctesiphon. A. Be silent about deadly desires, and leave aside the love-charms; I hate the playthings of which they speak, the gifts of the Sea-born. O. We hear that you, blessed one, are uninitiated in marriage. A. Sing of the battles of beasts and of hunting men; sing of the breeds of hounds and the varied tribes of horses, their swift-witted counsels, the deeds of profitable tracking; the hatreds among beasts are mine to tell, their loves to sing, and the bridal chambers in the mountains of tearless Cythera, and the births among beasts of unmidwifed travail. Such are the commands of the daughter of great Zeus. I have heard, I sing; may I cast a voice that strikes the mark. But you, who reign from the East to the Ocean, glad beneath your ambrosial brows in fair weather, extend your right hand, all-gracious, the giver of wealth, to the land and to the cities and to songs of good hunting.

A threefold hunting the god granted to men, the hunting of the air, of the land, and the lovely hunting of the sea; but the contest is not equal. For how can it be matched, to draw a gasping fish up from the depths, and to pull the long-winged birds down from the air, or to wrestle with murderous beasts in the mountains? Yet not even for the fisherman, and not in vain for the fowler, is there a catch without toil; only delight attends the toil, that and no killing; for they remain unstained by blood. The one, seated on the rocks beside the sea with curving rods and with deadly hooks, the fearless angler binds fast the cunning fish; and his is the pleasure, when, having pierced it through the jaws with bronze, he carries through the air the sea-born dancer leaping high above the depths and gasping. Yes, and to the fowler the toil is sweet; for to the hunt he carries no sword, no sickle, no bronze spears, but with him as a companion to the thickets goes the hawk, and the long cords and the soft honey-coloured birdlime, and the reeds that tread the airy path. Who could dare to sing that these are of equal weight? Or who would set the eagle against the lion king? With the poison of leopards who would compare the moray, or jackals with hawks, or rhinoceroses with sea-urchins, or the gull with wild goats, or all the sea-monsters with the elephant? Hunters have slain wolves, fishermen tunny; trappers have taken sheep, fowlers doves; pursuers the bear, and anglers the mormyr; horsemen the tiger, and harpooners the red mullet; trackers the boar, and birdlimers nightingales. But you, Nereus, and you spirits of Amphitrite, and you choir of bird-loving Dryads, be gracious; for now the songs I love call me eagerly back, and I turn to sing of the beast-slaying spirits.

First, let the hunters not be too fat for me; for there is great need to leap a towering horse over the crags, need too to vault the trench. And often in the thickets one must drive the beast, nimble of foot and light of limb. So let them not go fat to the toil of the hunt, nor yet too lean; for sometimes the much-hunting man must do battle with the warlike beasts. Therefore let them carry a body blended thus, both swift to run and strong to fight. And in the right hand let them brandish javelins, a pair of long ones, and a curved blade at the middle of the belt; for both let them prepare a bitter death for the beasts, and let them carry defences against evil men. In the left, the man on foot leads the hounds, the horseman guides the bridle that steers his horses. Let him fasten his tunic neatly up to the thigh and draw it in, girt tight with crossing belts. On either side of the neck let the cloak hang loose from the hands back behind over the strong shoulders, for easier labour; and let those go on bare feet who care for the hard-to-see tracks of beasts, so that the noise of sandals rubbed beneath oiled feet may not steal sleep from the eyes of the beasts. And let him not wear too ample a cloak; for a garment often stirred by the breath of a sounding wind has startled the beasts, and they have sprung up to flee. Thus let the hunters array their swift bodies well; for such Leto's daughter, the Archer, loves.

Let them go against the beasts at different hours, at the rising of the day, and at the day's decline, and at midday, and sometimes at evening; sometimes too in the dark they have subdued beasts beneath the rays of the moon. For the hunter the dawn is favourable on every side, all serene through the whole day's running, in leaf-bearing spring and in leaf-shedding autumn; for above all the temperate seasons are best for horses and men and ravening hounds to run in, in golden spring, the driver-away of chilly clouds, when the sea is passable for seafarers who sail it, who spread the white gear of the sail-winged ships; when the earth rejoices for men who tend their plants; when she loosens the bonds of buds and blossoms; or again at the last turning-points of autumn, when the house of the fruit-gathering farmer flourishes, when Athena's fruit fills the gleaming oil-jar and the cluster of the vines, pressed, gladdens the wine-vats, when the lily honeycombs weigh down the bee-hives. In midwinter let them hunt at the middle of the day, when in the thickets someone, withdrawn beneath a cave, having gathered dry sticks and kindled a quick-dying flame, the herdsman, leaning near the fire, has made ready his meal. In summer one must flee the flaming threat and the parching of the sun; and I bid them come to the contest at the first twilight, when at dawn the farmers beneath the well-made ploughtail, below the plough-beam, drive the earth-cleaving plough with their oxen; or again in the evening when the sun lowers the yoke, when the herdsmen give the signal to their flocks, when they go back again toward their own folds, heavy with milk and churning their udders; and the young, darting eagerly from the stony stalls, all frisk around their own dear mothers, the grim-eyed calves about the bright-eyed cows, the lambs about the well-horned ewes that bleat, the kids about the bleating goats, and the foals about the swift mares. And let the strong toilers carry to the slopes and the woods so many weapons of the glorious hunt, gear that breathes great slaughter of good hunting: well-twisted nets and withes and the long all-catching seine, nets and forked stakes and the much-groaning bonds of snares, the three-pronged spear, the broad-headed hunting-lance, the noose and the poles and the swift well-feathered arrow, swords and ox-axes and the hare-killing trident, crooked hooks and lead-weighted curved barbs, the cord bound with esparto and the well-plaited foot-snare, the meshes and the stakes and the many-eyed dragnet.

Let them lead to the hunt horses of great renown, the males; not only because the females are weaker in foot for running the long course in the woods, but because one must avoid the bed-loving heart of swift-footed horses, and keep the mare far off, so that they may not neigh in longing for love, and the fawns and swift gazelles and the timid hare, hearing it, run off in cold rout. Of horses there are gleaming tribes, as many as the countless races of men, all the breeds that, parcelled out among mortals, eat bread; but nevertheless I will tell which among all are strong, and which excel among the bands of horses: Tyrrhenians, Sicilians, Cretans, Mazices, Achaeans, Cappadocians, Moors, Scythians, Magnesians, Epeians, Ionians, Armenians, Libyans, Thracians, Erembi. A horse pre-eminent among all they have marked, those skilled in race-courses and the keepers of herds, one whose whole body is crowned with such features as these: let him lift a little above the neck his head held high aloft, though he himself is large, with rounded limbs; his head held high, his lower jaw inclined toward the neck; let his brow be broad and bright between the eyes; and from the temple about the forehead let thick clusters of hair shake; the eye keen, fiery, fierce beneath the brows; wide nostrils, a sufficient mouth, small ears; let the neck of the shaggy-maned horse be curved, as when the maned helmet bends its crest; let his chest be broad, his body long, his back wide, and a double spine fattening the haunches in the middle; and let a thick long-haired tail stream out behind; the thighs well-knit, muscular; but below straight and long and rounded are the cannons of the legs and very slender; the limbs lean of flesh, like those of long-horned, storm-footed deer; let the pastern slope, and let the round hoof run high off the ground, dense, horny, strong. Such a horse let me ride into the strong war of beasts, spirited, my fellow-toiler, warlike, mighty. Such are the Tyrrhenian and the Armenian and the Achaean, and the famous Cappadocian and those who dwell before the Taurus. A great marvel I have seen in the swift-footed Cappadocians: as long as they bear the new tooth in their mouths and a milk-fed body, they are weak; but they grow swifter the more they age. Arm those for great-hearted war and against the fiery beasts; for, very bold, they meet weapons, break the close phalanx, and fight face to face with the warlike beasts. For how, in battles, has the warlike horse endured the war-rousing din of the long trumpets? Or how with unblinking eyes has he looked straight at warriors, an ambush packed with men-at-arms, and the gleaming bronze, and the flashing iron, and learned when he must stand fast and when again to charge, and learned to heed the watchword of the strong captains? Often too he has charged at the towers of fighting men, calm beneath the winged roof of shields, when for mortals shield against shield is set crosswise above the head, when they long to sack the city of their enemies, and make a high plain of seven ox-hides, intricate, dense, many-bossed, and against the gleam of bronze the sunlit flash leaps back, and at once behind the brightness, as the ray slants away, the wide sky lightens. For to horses cunning Nature gave beyond all the heart of mortal creatures and a quick-changing spirit in their breasts: they always know their own dear charioteer and neigh when they see their glorious leader, and greatly lament a comrade fallen in battle. A horse once in the fray broke the bonds of silence and overran the laws of nature and took a human voice and a tongue like that of men. The horse of the warlike Macedonian king, Bucephalas, fought face to face against the weapons. A horse once ran on the ears of corn with light feet, another over the sea, and did not wet his fetlock-band. A horse carried above the clouds the slayer of the Chimaera, and a neighing colt once, through the tricks of its groom, made the Persian, the Asian-born, a king. Above all too they honour their nature; and it is utterly unheard-of for them to come to a love that is not lawful; but they remain unstained by defilement, and desire only pure Cythera. I have heard how once one of the wealthy lords kept on his plains a fair herd of horses; and afterwards a horse-plague, subduing them all root and branch, left but two, the mother alone and her dear mother's still suckling foal. But when he was grown, the cruel man tried to lay the mother in the embrace of her own son. And when he saw them refusing love and marriage abhorred by both, then straightway, plotting dread things, he wove a crafty scheme, hoping to call back the breed again to his horses. First he covered both, brooding mischief, with other hides; then he anointed their whole bodies with sweet-smelling, fragrant oil; for he hoped to blot out the scent, the guide to love; and he succeeded, O blessed gods, in working evil; and it was accomplished, a strange bed, abominable, most hateful to horses, such as was wed among men of old, the dread Cadmean marriage of wandering Oedipus. But when, uncovered, they saw their ruin, and looked at each other in anguish with sidelong eyes, she, wretched, at the unborn offspring, and he straightway, ill-wed, ill-bedded, at his pitiable motherless mother, they reared high aloft, snorting savagely, and breaking their bonds they went, neighing loud, as if calling the blessed gods to witness their misery, and praying curses upon the bringer of so much woe; and at last, weeping and rushing wildly, driving their heads against the rocks opposite, they crushed their bones together and put out their own light, self-slain, leaning their heads upon each other. So report sings great glory of the horses of old. Of all the breeds of horses that the boundless earth has reared, the swiftest are the Sicilians who dwell about Lilybaeum and the three-headed mountain where, the covering of Enceladus, belching with fiery flashes of the thunderbolt, the everlasting fire of Sicilian Etna boils up. Swifter than the Sicilians, beside the streams of the Euphrates, are the Armenians and the deep-haired Parthians. But the Iberians far surpass even the Parthians, striking the plain with swifter feet. With them perhaps only the eagle could match itself, the eagle driving through the hollows of the air, or the hawk shaken on long wings, or the dolphin gliding through the grey surge. So swift of foot, so windlike, are the Iberians; but they are few and small in strength and weak of heart, and proved wanting in a course of but a few stades; their forms are clothed in splendid beauty and a glorious body, but their hoof is not strong, clay-bred, broad-soled. The gleaming tribes of the Moors far surpass all in long courses and in painful labours. And the Libyans next to them run the long course, all those who dwell about Cyrene rich in pebbles. The forms of both are alike, except that the Libyans are larger to look upon and grow up strong, but long in body; for about their flanks they have, more than the others, a broad rib-cage; and therefore they are thicker to look upon and better at charging straight, and good at bearing the fiery rush of the sun and the sharp midday threat of thirst. The Tyrrhenian horses and the boundless Cretan tribes are both swift to run and long of body. Swifter than the Moors are the Sicilians, and than the Sicilians the Parthians, and they are bright-eyed and exceedingly gleaming, and they alone endure the great roar of the lion. For indeed against different beasts different breeds of horses are fitted, as their colours show you. Against the dappled-footed deer arm yourself with dark-eyed horses, grey ones against bears, and tawny against leopards, fiery, flame-bright horses against boars, but bright-eyed grey ones against grey-eyed lions. In beauty above all is the horse pre-eminent, the Nesaean, which wealthy kings bring; fair to see, gentle to carry on an obedient rein; small of head, but full in his deep-haired neck, glorying on either side with honey-golden mane. Yes, and you may behold another lovely breed, dappled, conspicuous, which they call the Orynges, either because they grow up in the fair-tressed mountains, or because they are wholly eager to leap upon the females. A twofold many-flowered beauty belongs to the Orynges: for some have neck and fair-haired wide backs inscribed close with long stripes, like swift tigers, the offspring of swift Zephyr; others are wrought with rounded spots all about, with close seal-marks like leopards; these, while they were still young, skilled men marked, searing the long hair with burning bronze. Often men have devised another all-cunning thing, to mark the colt even while it was in the mother's womb. Oh how great is the heart, how great the mind in men! They did as they wished; they made horses of many colours while still wrapped in the milky flanks of the mother. For when a longing for love seizes the female horse and she awaits a famous high-spirited stallion coming near, then they adorn the fair mate; and all about his whole body they paint with well-dappled colours, and lead him to the bed, proud in his splendour. And as some young man, by the bridal-tending women crowned with white garments and purple flowers, and breathing of Palestinian perfume, enters the chamber singing the bridal-song; so the horse, hastening and neighing the marriage-strain, the famous mate foaming before his bride, they long restrain, eager for the beloved bed; and late at last they release him to the lovely union; and she, conceiving, bears a many-coloured foal, having taken in her womb the fruitful seed of the male, but received the colour with her eyes, many-hued. Such things too those men, who have care of the reeds, the fowlers, contrived with subtle thoughts, when they adorn the nestlings of the ring-doves; for when the swift wood-pigeons go to love, mingling with their deep-voiced mates, then the bird-keeper weaves his famous scheme, and beside the females he sets many embroidered things, purple garments; and they, casting their eyes aside in desire, warmed in their hearts, bring forth sea-purple young. Yes, and thus the Laconians devised a clever thing for their own dear wives, when they swell in the womb: painting on tablets they set near them splendid beauties, those who once flashed bright among men as youths, Nireus and Narcissus and Hyacinthus of the good ash-spear, Castor of the fair helm and Polydeuces slayer of Amycus, and the young men who are admired among the blessed gods, laurel-haired Phoebus and ivy-bearing Dionysus; and the women delight to see the much-loved form, and bear fair children, gazing upon beauty.

So much about horses; but come down, dear heart, to the path of the hounds. So many among all dogs are pre-eminently splendid and dear to hunters: Paeonians, Ausonians, Carians, Thracians, Iberians, Arcadians, Argives, Lacedaemonians, Tegeans, Sauromatians, Celts, Cretans, Magnesians, Amorgians, and all who upon the sandy banks of Egypt are keepers of herds, Locrians, and grey-eyed Molossians. And if it is your pleasure to blend two breeds, in spring first prepare the bed for hounds; for in spring more than at other times the works of love are the care of beasts and hounds and deadly serpents and birds of the air and the swimming creatures of the sea. In spring the viper, smeared with angry venom, came to the shore to the bed of his sea-dwelling mate; in spring the whole sea resounds for Cytherea, and the swimming creatures, mating, shudder the calm with ripples; in spring too the wood-pigeons pair with the doves, and horses are armed for the field-haunting mares, and bulls rush upon the wild heifers, and the curl-horned rams in spring mount the sheep, and the fiery boars rage among the sows, and the shaggy he-goats ride the she-goats; and to men themselves in spring loves come more strongly; for in spring Cytherea, who belongs to all, presses upon them.

Let the tribes of dogs be your care, you who tend the bridal, breeds fitted to each other and the surpassing kinds. Mix Arcadians with Eleans, Cretans with Paeonians, Carians with Thracians, Tyrrhenian breeds with Laconians, and you may bring a Sarmatian mate to an Iberian bride. Thus you would blend them well; but far the best of all are the breeds that remain unmixed, which the huntsmen have judged supreme; and the tribes are countless, of whatever origin; and let their shapes and forms be such as this. A long, strong, sturdy body, and a head light, bright-eyed; let the dark eyes glitter; let the jagged mouth be wide; let the small ears above be wrapped in thin membranes; the neck long, and the chest beneath strong, broad; and let the forelegs be the shorter pair; straight and long and tall be the masts of the limbs; broad the shoulder-blades, the ribs slanting crosswise; the loins fleshy, not fat; but behind let the tail be firm and long, casting a long shadow. Such hounds let be armed for the long courses, against gazelles and deer and the storm-footed hare. Others again are fierce, in whom is staunch courage, which have set upon well-bearded bulls and rushing on insolent boars have slain them; which do not even dread lions, their own kings, well-fed, like jutting hilltops; they are flatter in the face, and dreadfully above the brow droops between the eyes, and fiery eyes glitter beneath grey-glancing lids; the whole hide is shaggy; the body strong; the back broad; they are not swift, but the strength within them is great, and their power unspeakable, pure, and their spirit shameless. For the hunt then arm yourself with such breeds of warrior hounds, which pursue all beasts. Colours both white and very dark are bad; for they can endure neither the swift force of the sun nor the force of the snow-stricken, wintry season. Those excel among all hounds whose forms are most like the ravening beasts, the sheep-slaying wolves or the windswift tigers, or the swift foxes and the leopards, or all those that have a form altogether like Demeter, corn-coloured; for they are very swift and strong. And if you have a wise care for the rearing of hounds, never let the whelps be suckled at the fresh-flowing teat of goats or sheep, nor by house-dogs; for so they would be sluggish and worthless and heavy; but at the teat of a deer, or perhaps a tamed lioness, or perhaps of gazelles, or of the night-roaming she-wolf; for so you would make them especially strong and swift, like the very milk-giving nurses themselves. And to the young whelps give names that are short, all quick, so that they may hear the quick call. Let them from puppyhood be companions of the strong hunting horses, and to all men familiar and friendly, hostile only to the beasts. Let them not wish to bark; for to hunters silence is the rule, and above all for the trackers.

Two kinds there are of the hard-to-see tracking, of men and of hounds; men of shifting counsel have judged by their eyes and marked out the paths; but hounds with their nostrils have noted every track. Yes, and for men the winter season is favourable, and they track with effortless eyes, because in the snow all things are seen marked together, and in the mud they remain stamped like footprints. But spring is hateful to hounds, and autumn is dear; for in spring the grass-feeding earth, full of herbage, abounds with flowers and is full of scents, and all about the well-crowned meadows grow purple unploughed, and the fields, with their dominant odour, blot out for the keen-scented hounds the trail upon the trackways; but in fruitful autumn with its sweet clusters the grasses and the herbs and the flowers grow old, and the scent of the beast remains bare for the hounds.

There is a brave breed of tracking hounds, small, but worthy of a great song; the wild tribes of the Britons with their painted backs reared them, and by surname they called them Agassaei. Their size indeed is like that of the worthless greedy little table-dogs of the house, crooked, most fleshless, shaggy-haired, dull of eye, but armed in the feet with grievous claws and furnished with close-set venomous fangs; but in the nostrils above all the Agassaeus is supreme and best at tracking; for both, when they go on the ground, he is very skilled to find the track, and skilled too to mark even the airy scent itself. And when one of the hunters, longing to test his hound, before the steep gates carries in his hands a hare, dead or alive, he creeps forward sideways along the path, first straight, then driving it crooked, to the left, to the right, winding the twisting road about; but when he has come very far from the city and the gates, then digging a pit he buries it; and returning back to the city, at once he leads near the path the cunning hound; and it straightway is stirred, and snorts at the hare's scent; it seeks the tracks along the ground, and longing to find them cannot at all; and greatly vexed it wanders about. And as when a girl, in the tenth month of the moon, a first-time mother stricken by the pangs of childbirth, has loosed her braids and loosed the ornaments from her breasts, and tunicless, wretched, with no veil upon her head, wanders everywhere through the house, and in her labour now goes to the forecourt, now again makes straight for the bed, now flung in the dust wails, rubbing her rosy cheeks; so he, vexed with heart-devouring pains, darts this way and that and in turn searches every stone and every hill and every path, the trees and the vines and the walls and the threshing-floors. But when at last he chances upon the airy track, he laughs and whines for joy, just as the little calves frisk about the udder-rich cows; so his heart too rejoices, and rushing on he wheels about, set upon the winding plains; nor could you turn him aside, not even if you drove him far off; he makes straight, clinging fast to the sweet scent, until he passes to the end of the toil and to the starting-line. And if you arm him against unhunted hares, he draws near secretly, and presses track upon track, small, hidden among vines or stalks, like a thief who steals kids, who, when the herdsman sleeps nearby, watching, creeps up quietly. But when he has drawn near the lairs of the hares, swiftly he springs, like a bow or a hissing serpent, which the reaper or some ploughman has roused, as it lay quiet before in its arrow-holding hole. So he, exulting, sprang swiftly; and if he succeeds, easily, having mastered it with his sharper claws and seized it in his jaws, he would meet you with the great burden; swiftly he carries it, toiling and weighed down, and draws near. And as from the cornfield the wagon brings the harvest of reaping, laden with wheat, and goes toward the farmstead, and the farmers, seeing it, rush all together, and meeting it in front, one props the wheels, another the body of the cart, another helps the axle for the oxen; and coming to the farmstead they loose the plough-beam, and the oxen, sweating, take breath from their toil, and the heart of the weary herdsman greatly rejoices; so he comes, bringing the burden in his jaws. And the swift hunter meets him, rejoicing, and lifting both high off the ground from the mother, sets in his bosom the prey and the beast-slayer himself.

Come now, daughter of Zeus, fair-ankled Phoebe, maiden of the golden girdle, twin offspring with Apollo, tell me which of men and mighty heroes lifted from your hand the far-famed lore of the hunt. About the feet of windy Pholoe the wild tribes, the beast-mingled tribes, men down to the loins, and from the loins below half-human horses, found in hunting their evening meal. Among men the first who reaped the Gorgon's neck, Perseus, the famous son of golden Zeus, devised it; but, raised on the swift wings of his feet, he seized both hares and jackals and the race of wild goats and swift gazelles and the breeds of antelopes and the very lofty heads of dappled deer. The mounted hunt the light-bringing Castor devised; and some he slew, striking straight with the well-aimed javelin, and others again, driving on swift horses, he took the beasts at the meeting-points of the midday course. For battles against beasts jagged-toothed hounds the Zeus-born Lacedaemonian Polydeuces first armed; for in boxing he slew dread men and with swift hounds he subdued the dappled beasts. Above all in the lists of the mountain contests the warlike son of Oeneus, Meleager, flashed forth. Nets again and nooses and the curved meshes first Hippolytus revealed to hunting men. And the famous daughter of Schoeneus, Atalanta, the boar-slaying maiden, found the winged death for beasts. Nightly snares, the all-cunning hunt of night, Orion, crafty of mind, first devised. So many were the strong leaders of the hunt of old. But many afterward keen love subdued; for no one, mastered by the goads of the lovely hunt, would willingly leave it again; unspeakable bonds hold him fast. How sweet is sleep upon the flowers in spring, and how sweet again in summer the lowly couch in a cave, and what delight there is on the crags for hunters to take their fill; and how great is the grace that attends them, as they themselves pluck the bloom of honey-sweet autumn; and the cold white water poured forth from the cave, what sweet drink and bath it is for the weary; and what welcome gifts they bring back in the thickets in sweet baskets from the goatfolds, the herdsmen.

But come now, let us first sing of the wholly jealous breed of bulls, and the countless and surpassing strife they waged, all wild, over the bridal-bed. One king, ruling the herd, far the best, lords it over the lesser bulls and the females; the herd trembles before its great horned leader, and the wild cattle dread their savage mate, whenever he bellows. But when, parted from the herd, another bull, stretching out his broad neck, goes off alone, himself a king ruling his own, then over them both an overpowering war is set. First, looking face to face at one another, they rage wildly with hot-tempered wrath and flash great fire, and breathe forth flame, and tear the earth with their feet, as if covering themselves with dust; from either side they challenge, crying sharply with warlike shouts. But when they have sounded the trumpet for the grievous battle, they rush unrestrained, and at once with their horns they wound each other's whole bodies in turn. And as in a sea-battle, when war upon the waves raises its strife, two ships pre-eminent, flashing with thick-set warriors against the foe, clash prow against prow face to face, driven by the fierce blast and the hands of the sailors; and about the bronze armour rings the din of men and of shattered ships; all Nereus groans with the swell; such a din from the bulls too reaches the sky, as they strike untiringly and are struck by the horns, until at last one wins the dear victory that turns the tide. But the loser bears no slavish yoke; ashamed and groaning heavily he comes to the shadowy wood; and alone among the crags, as the years come round, he feeds, withdrawn in the mountain-haunting thickets, like one in training; and when he sees his strength grown mighty and his power a match for the other, at once he cries out from the hills; and the other answers, and the wood resounds; but when he has taken courage in his stronger cries, then straight from the mountains he comes against his foe, and easily wins; for he has trained his body with pasture far off in the thickets, away from strength-marring Cythera.

Many are the forms and countless the ways of bulls. By the bright-fruited banks of Egypt's Nile, the wheat-bearing, many-channelled river, there are bulls snow-white in colour, by far the greatest of all in size; you would say a deep-keeled ship was moving over the land; gentle they are in spirit and familiar with men, for, since mortals tend them, kindly they submit. The Phrygian bulls are conspicuous in colour, yellow and flame-bright; deep is the flesh on their necks; and on top a rounded mane stands high aloft. A strange nature is fashioned in their horns; for they are not fixed firm above the head, but they slope their horns and bend them to either side. The Aonian are single-hoofed, a dappled breed, one-horned, and from the middle of the forehead a dread horn rises up. The Armenians have a double horn, but curling in shape, a great affliction, twisted backward with their spear-points. The Syrian bulls, the breed of the Chersonese, who dwell about steep, well-built Pella, are tawny, strong, great-hearted, broad-browed, field-haunting, sturdy, strong-horned, fierce of spirit, loud-bellowing, grim, jealous, broad-jawed; but they are not fat to weigh down their ample bodies, nor again lean and feeble in body; thus they bear the famous gifts of the gods, blended, both swift to run and strong to fight: those which, the tale was, Heracles, the son of Zeus, mighty in his labours, drove of old from Erytheia, when on Ocean he fought against Geryon and slew him on the crags; for he was to accomplish another labour, not for Hera nor at the commands of Eurystheus, but for his comrade Archippus, leader of holy Pella. For of old, before the feet of Emblonus, the whole plain was flooded; for great Orontes ever sped onward in haste, and forgot the grey sea, burning for the dark-eyed nymph, daughter of Ocean; he lingered among the rocks, and covered the fertile land, unwilling to leave the ill-starred longing for Meliboea. On both sides he was ringed round by encircling mountains, which on either hand stretched their heads against each other; from the east came the lofty form of Diocleium, and from the west the left horn of Emblonus, while he himself, rushing in the midst of the plains, ever swelling and journeying near the wall, poured his waters over the mainland and the island alike, my own city. Therefore the son of Zeus was straightway to measure out for both the streams with his club and his mighty hands, and to guide the waters apart from the plain, of the fair-tressed lake and the well-wheeling river. He performed a mighty labour, for he cut through the crown of the encircling mountains, and loosed the stony bonds, and let the river forth, belching at its outlets, swelling unrestrained and roaring wild, and guided it to the shores; and the loud sea roared, and the dark body of the Syrian beach resounded. Not such, on either side of the loud-roaring sea, are the two opposing rivers that descend with their fierce water; on one side the Ister, cutting the white reins of Boreas, through Scythia roars greatly everywhere on every hand, dragged along by cliffs and water-beaten headlands; on the other the holy stream of Egypt from Libya, breaking about it, makes the far-sounding sea tremble. So the great river Orontes gurgled round the shores with a terrible roar; and hugely the shores cried out as they received in their bays the swell of the new-come sea; and the dark-skinned, udder-rich land took breath, rising up from the wave, the new field of Heracles. Everywhere even now the fields wave with corn-ears, everywhere the works of oxen weigh down the teeming threshing-floors about the Memnonian shrine, where the Assyrian dwellers lament Memnon, the famous offspring of the early-born Dawn, whom once, when he came to help the sons of Priam, the bold husband of Deidameia swiftly subdued. But these wide beauties of our homeland we shall sing in due order with the lovely Pimpleian strain; now I turn back to the famous song of the hunt.

There is an irresistible breed among the murderous bulls, which they call Bisons; for they come from the homeland of Bistonian Thrace; and they have got such forms as these: a bristling mane they shake over their shoulders, on fat necks and about their soft chins; just as the shaggy lions, lords of beasts, yellow-haired and grim, have a conspicuous look; and the sharp points of their fire-tipped horns are like curved bronze hooks; but, not as in other beasts, opposite one another the points of the hateful horns lean crosswise, and the deadly goads look upward to the sky. Therefore, whenever they come up with and reach either a man or some beast, they lift it high aloft. Their tongue is narrow but exceedingly rough, like the work of iron-devouring iron; and with their tongue, drawing blood, they lick the flesh away.

Yes, and the earth has reared the breed of swift-footed deer, fair-horned, large-eyed, conspicuous, dapple-backed, spotted, splendid, river-crossing, high-headed, fat in the back and slender in the legs; worthless is the neck and very small again the tail; fourfold the nostrils, four the channels for the breath; feeble the heart and the spirit weak within, and the points of their horns rise up, but blunt; for never would they fight head to head, not against strong beasts, nor against grievous hounds, nor even against the very cowardly shaggy-shanked hares. But rough is the love of deer and great their Aphrodite, and their spirit toward the bed burns the whole day long, like that of the ever-rutting fighting cocks and all the flower-plumaged, feather-clad birds. In their flanks within, beneath the very belly, they hide twin ducts; and if one should cut these away, at once he makes the male a female, and reaps from its head the sharp-haired, much-wrought, dappled growth of horns. Not as with other beasts is the marriage-law for the bed of these, but strange desires are their care; for neither standing in the field-haunting glens, nor reclining on the low flowers of the grass do they bed in company with the female deer, but, running on swift feet, he overtakes her as she runs; and as she flees he seizes and holds his mate in his arms; yet even so he does not persuade her; carrying her husband on her back she steadily flees, with an utterly merciless heart; but he, following on his two nimble feet, does not let go his desire, and fulfils the laws of wedlock. But when afterward, as the months come round, the female gives birth, she avoids the path of men, because the trodden ways of mortals are profane to beasts. Above all among beasts they pride themselves on their splendour, the fair-horned males, having the much-wrought growth; for indeed when the well-cloven horns fall in their season, they dig a pit in the earth and bury them, so that no one may find them, meeting with them in the furrow; and they themselves hide in the innermost shaggy thickets, ashamed to appear before the beasts with such heads, bare, which before were raised aloft. Amphibious are deer; for they tread the dry land and also cross the sea, swimming in convoy with one another a seafaring voyage, when they make their way over the sea; in front one leads the deer along the lines, like a helmsman handling the rudder of a ship; and another, leaning his back behind upon him, follows with his neck and head, crossing the sea; and so, one bearing another, they cut the sea. But when first weariness seizes the one swimming, he leaves the line and comes to the rear of the column, and rests, leaning on another, a little from his toil; and another in turn takes the rudder and journeys over the sea; and all, as they swim, leaders by turns, with their feet, as with oars, row the dark water, and lift on high the lovely form of their horns, as if entrusting to the winds the sails of a ship. A relentless hatred toward one another they ever have, the whole race of serpents and of deer; and everywhere the deer in the mountain glens searches out the bold creeper. But when it sees, woven in long coils, the serpent's track, exulting greatly it comes near the den, and sets its nostrils to the hole, drawing on with fierce breath to battle the deadly reptile; and the one unwilling to fight it forces out by its breath from the innermost bed; for at once it sees its foe, and lifts high to the air its baleful neck; and it bares its white teeth, sharply bristling; and the venom-bearing beast clatters its jaws, hissing with thick-set whistlings. But straightway the deer, like one smiling, carves with its mouth the foe fighting in vain, and as it writhes about its knees and about its neck steadily devours it; and over the ground are poured many quivering, gasping remnants in slaughter. And you might soon pity, savage though it is, the flesh-eater, flung in much-mangled slaughter. On the borders of horse-feeding Libya there roams a vast, deadly, gleaming host of creeping things; but when the deer, reclining on the sandy headlands, is alone, at once from all sides the hostile swarm of countless serpents rushed upon it, and the hateful battalions, venom-bearing; and they fastened their bitter teeth in its hide, poured all about, standing round all the deer's joints; for some, turning their heads from above, gnaw with their jaws the brows and forehead, others the slender neck and the chest beneath and the flanks and belly they carve through with their mouths, others again cling to the ribs on either side, others feed upon the thighs and the back above, and one and another hangs fixed, hostile, from this side and that. But the deer, encompassed with pains of every kind, first wishes to escape on its swift feet, but has not the strength; such a marvellous throng, gleaming and ruinous, of creeping things besets it. Then, weighed down, it stands fast under strong necessity, and devours with its mouth the boundless hostile tribes, roaring with pain; and turning this way and that it ravages the creeping race, sparing none. And they do not let go, but, perishing, hold fast, having a stubborn heart in the shamelessness of their minds; and some it tears with its jaws, and others with its feet and hooves it slays, and over the earth runs endlessly the bloody ichor from the serpents; and the limbs of the beasts and their half-eaten joints quiver on the ground; others again, half-mangled, it crushes against its ribs; for even dead they still hold fast with their strong teeth, and only their heads, fixed in the hide, remain shut tight. But it, knowing the gift it has received from the god, searches everywhere for the dark stream of a river; there, having mastered crabs with its dear jaws, it has a self-taught remedy for the woeful ruin; and at once the remnants of the bitter beasts fall to the earth from its hide, rolling of themselves down past its feet, and the wounds on either side close up over the teeth. And the deer lives again a long time; and in truth the race of men has named it the four-crows-aged. Others again men call broad-horned; they are wholly deer, but above they bear such a nature of horns as the name proclaims to those beasts. And there are those they call iorci in the thickets; these too have the body of a deer, and on the back a hide all spotted they bear, all-dappled, just as the seal-marks of leopards gleam upon the skin. The Bubalus again is smaller in body than the broad-horned, smaller than the broad-horned, but far better than the gazelle; bright of eye, lovely of hue, fair to look upon; and his horns grow straight from the head, the points stretched forward, and then again up toward the back they bend backward with their inward-curving tips. Above all this tribe loves its own home, its familiar couches and its dear lair in the glens; and if hunters, having bound it with twisted snares, should lead it at once to other regions, and far off in the glens leave it free there, easily it comes back to its sweet home, where it dwelt, nor would it endure to wander, a stranger, in foreign lands. Not to men alone, then, is the homeland dear; some longing too is instilled in the hearts of the dappled beasts.

Yes, and the conspicuous breeds of the swiftest gazelles, their form, their size, and their strength we all know alike. The fierce partridges, fiery-eyed, gleaming-necked, have made friendship with the gazelles in the loved glens, and they are familiar and share one home with one another, and have their couches close, and do not feed apart. Truly afterward they soon tasted bitter comradeship and joyless friendship, when cunning men devised against the wretched creatures a clever thing, making the partridges a snare for their dear gazelles, and again the gazelles in turn a snare for their partridge friends. Of goats again and of sheep there are wild tribes, not much larger than these fleecy sheep and shaggy goats, but swift to run and strong to fight, armed on the head with twisted horns. The strength of the sheep again is in their grievous foreheads; often, charging in the thickets, they have laid even rushing boars gasping on the ground. There are times when, charging face to face at one another, they fight; and a mighty din reaches the sky; nor is it lawful for them to avoid the foe, but to bear off victory from one another is unshakable necessity, or to lie a corpse; such strife has arisen for them. In the wild goats there is, through the very teeth, a slender pipe of breath, in the midst of the horns, whence then straight to the very heart and lungs it goes; and if one should pour wax about a wild goat's horns, he has shut off the paths of life and the channels of breath. Above all the mother tends her young, still tender babes, her children; and in old age the children tend the mother. As mortals, when their father is fettered in the grievous bonds of old age, heavy in foot, shrunken of limb, feeble of hand, trembling of body, dim of sight, cherish him and hold him very dear above all, repaying the care of their own grievous rearing; so the kids of goats tend their dear parents when old, when the much-groaning bonds fetter their limbs; they offer them dewy, flowery fodder, plucked with their mouths; and drink with their lip-tips they bring from the river, drawing up the dark water; and tending all the body with their tongue they make it bright. And if you should take the mother alone in your snares, at once you would take in your hands also the new-suckling lambs; for you would think she was driving off her children with words, beseeching them with such bleatings from afar: "Flee from me, dear children, the foe-meeting hunters, lest, subdued, you make me a wretched, childless mother." You would think she said such things; and those standing before her first, you would say, sing a mournful strain about their mother, and then utter a human voice, breaking into a bleat, and from their mouths cry out such words, like those who speak and like those who beseech: "By Zeus we beseech you, by the Archer-goddess herself, release for me my dear mother, and accept this ransom, all that we, wretched, can bring for our pitiable mother, we, ill-fated; bend your savage heart, in reverence for the law of the blessed gods and your father's old age, if indeed a father is left to you in your gleaming home." Such things you would think they say in their pleading. But when they behold a heart utterly merciless, oh how great is their shame, how great their longing for their parents! self-bound they walk and of their own accord they pass over. There are yellow sheep at the farthest ends of Crete, in the low Gortynian land, four-horned; a purple fleece is wreathed about their skin, thick and not soft; it would soon rival a goat's with its rough hair, hard to handle, not a sheep's. Such a yellow-faced look the soubus has, gleaming in colour, but no longer shaggy, nor again fitted with four horns, but with two strong ones above its very broad forehead. Amphibious too is the soubus, for it also journeys by sea; for whenever it goes to the deep, cleaving the swift waves, then a great throng, journeying together over the sea, a fishy company, follows, and licks its joints, delighting in their dear horned one, the tender-skinned soubus. Above all the sea-breams and the worthless melanuri and the needle-fish and red mullets and lobsters follow round about. A marvel this was, a marvel unspeakable, when beasts are afflicted by strange longings and surpassing love-charms. For not only toward one another a law of equal love, a binding ordinance, did the god give, nor only so far that their tribe should grow up in everlasting life. A marvel, then, is that too, that mindless tribes are subdued by lovely bonds and learn kindred love-charms, and mingle in one another a desire they do not understand, just as for men understanding and mind opened the eyes and received love in the heart; but even in alien love-charms they rage on high. Such is the longing of the conspicuous deer for the woodcocks; how great upon the long-horned gazelles is the partridges' love; and how again in swift horses the bustards delight, whose ear is ever most shaggy; again the parrot and the wolf feed with one another; for ever the wolves long for the grass-coloured bird. Mighty Love, how great you are, how boundless your strength, how many things you devise, how much you rule, how much, O god, you play! The earth is fixed, yet by your shafts it is shaken; unstable is the sea, yet you have fixed even that; you came to the upper air, and great Olympus feared you; all things dread you, and the wide heaven above, and all that is beneath the earth, and the wretched tribes of the dead, who drew beneath their lips the soothing water of Lethe and fled all pains, yet still shudder at you. By your might you pass even far off, as far as the shining sun never beholds; and to your fire even the light yields, in fear, and the thunderbolts of Zeus alike yield. Such, O savage god, are the fiery arrows you have, piercing, ruinous, mind-destroying, maddening, breathing consumption, incurable, with which you have startled even the beasts themselves to unyoked desires. A marvel, when over the horned hind the winged woodcocks, leaping upon her dappled back, or the partridges on the gazelles, casting their thick wings, cool the sweat and soothe the spirit from the parching heat, fanning with their wings; or when before the loud-hoofed horse there goes the bustard, gliding lovely through the air, and the saragi fall upon the goatfolds; and about the soubus the whole wandering tribe of swimming creatures is stirred, and all follow together, when it cleaves the wild waves, and crowd together on either side rejoicing, and around the sea foams, shaken with their white fins; but it, caring nothing for the strange friendship, all-lawless, devours its sea-companions with bloody jaws, feasting; and they, seeing their doom before their eyes, not even so do they hate it, nor leave the slayer. Wretched soubus, evil-doer, against you yourself hereafter the hunters will prepare a sea-borne destruction, crafty though you are and a slayer of fish.

There is a sharp-horned beast that haunts the thickets, the fierce-spirited oryx, most chilling to beasts; its colour is like spring milk, only about the face with darkening cheeks; double behind are its haunches, fat with suet; and the sharp points of its horns rise up aloft, piercing, with a dark-coloured look, and they are stronger than sharpened bronze and chilling iron and jagged stone; and they say that nature is venom-bearing in those horns. The spirit again of the oryx is overweening and harsh; for it does not tremble at the barking of the keen-scented hound, nor at the snorting of the field-haunting boar among the crags, nor does it flee the strong bellowing of the bull, nor shudder at the joyless cry of leopards, nor flee the great roaring of the lion himself, nor heed men, in the shamelessness of its mind; often on the slopes a strong man has perished, a hunter, meeting the bloody oryx. But when the oryx beholds a strong-hearted beast, either a tusked boar or a jagged-toothed lion, or the deadly boldness of chilling bears, at once on the ground it droops its head and presses its forehead wholly down, stretched out, and fixing its bitter darts by the ground awaits the charging one, and slays it, killing first. For tilting its little horned forehead aslant, watching with sharper weapons, it falls upon the beast; but the beast cares not, and charges straight, irresistible, bristling with rage, pressing itself upon the sharp points. And as when, in the thickets, with a lion charging, a brave man graced with the gifts of Artemis, holding a flashing spear in his strong hands, stands firm with legs well astride, and receives the wild raging beast on the two-edged bronze held out before him; so the oryxes await the charging beasts then, self-slain, mastered by their own folly; for easily the points slip into their breasts, and much dark blood from the wounds on either side, pouring out, they soon lick with their tongues; nor is it possible for them to escape, even if they wish; but they destroy one another with mutual slaughter. And some field-dweller, or a herdsman, or some ploughman, meeting the twin corpses beside his feet, has a happy catch, with a heart of great wonder.

Next among the horned beasts it is fitting to sing the breeds of countless elephants; for they have in their jaws two overweening weapons, like tusks rising to the sky; others say these are the deadly teeth of the multitude, straying in error; but we are pleased to call them horns; for thus the nature of horns declares to us. The signs are not obscure to mark them apart; for in beasts the growths from the jaws above, all those that are horny, dart upward; but if they droop downward, plainly they are teeth. In those twin elephant horns the roots first grow from the head, great from the great, as in beasts; and then below, hidden by the hide, meeting at the temples, they are thrust into the jaw; and bared of the jaw they have given to most men a false notion of teeth. Yes, and another sign clear to men there was; for all the teeth in beasts are unbending, nor do they yield to art, but remain unsoftened; which, if the horn-carver should wish to make broad, they refuse outright; and if they are forced, they break short, unyielding; but from horns round bows and countless works are wrought; so those horns, which they call teeth, yield to be bent and widened by the ivory-cutters. The size of these beasts is such as no other beast upon the earth bears; you would say, seeing an elephant, that either a peak of a boundless mountain or a dread cloud bearing a storm for wretched men was journeying over the dry land. Mighty is the head upon smaller ears, hollow and smooth; but the eyes are smaller than that body warrants, great though they be. Between them runs out a great nose, slender and curved, which they call the trunk. This is the beast's hand; with this they do what they wish easily. But the measure of the feet is not equal; for in front they are lifted much higher. The hide again, hard to handle, covers the body, uncloven and strong, which not even the mighty, sharpened, all-subduing iron could cut through. Its spirit is boundless in the shadowy wood, savage; but among mortals it is tame and kind to men. In the green, many-slope glens it has stretched the oaks and wild olives and the high-headed breeds of date-palms, roots and all, upon the ground, striking them with its sharpened, boundless jaws; but when it comes into the strong hands of men, it forgets its spirit, and its savage heart leaves it; it endures the yoke and takes the bridle in its lips, and carries children on its back, masters of its tasks. There is a report that elephants speak to one another, muttering a human voice from their mouths; but the beast's cry is not audible to all, and only the men who tame them hear it. A marvel too I have heard, that the mightiest elephants have a prophetic heart in their breasts, and in their spirit know the necessity of their own death that is at hand. Not among birds alone, then, are there the prophetic swans that sing their last lament, but among beasts also this tribe, foreseeing its own end of death, makes ready its dirge.

The Rhinoceros has a body not much larger than the darting oryx, but a little above the tip of its nose there rises a dread horn, sharpened, a savage blade; with it, charging, it would pierce through bronze, and, wounding, would cleave a strong ravine. Even the strong elephant, when it has charged at it, it has often laid such a corpse in the dust. Faintly upon its yellow, fair-haired forehead and on its back the spots gleam purple in rows. All are males, and never is a female seen; and from where, I have not learned; but I tell as I have learned, whether from rock this deadly tribe has come, or whether they are earth-born and rise up from the ground, or whether from one another, a savage wonder, they are born without desires and without marriage and without birth. Already too in the wet depths of the water-traversing sea self-made and motherless tribes are bred, oysters and feeble small fry and the breeds of conchs, shells and whelks, which are born in the sands.

Dear Muse, it is not lawful for me to sing of small things; leave the worthless beasts, those that no strength attends, the grey-eyed panthers and the evil-doing wild cats, which arm themselves in dwelling-houses, and the small, tender, feeble dormice; these for the whole wintry season remain with eyes shut, their bodies drunk with sleep; luckless, neither taking food nor seeing the light; in their dens they have such sleep that they lie like corpses, having drawn a wintry doom. But when the first eyes of spring laugh, and the flowers in the meadows newly come to bloom, they move their sluggish bodies from the innermost lair, and open their eyes and behold the light of the sun, and remember the new delight of sweet food, and again they become alive and once more are dormice. I leave also the shaggy race of the worthless squirrel, which in the flaming hours of midsummer raises its tail as a shelter, a self-roofing dwelling; just as the peacocks shade their splendid form, painted, conspicuous, dapple-backed; than which the counsel of Zeus has devised nothing more delightful for men to behold with bright eyes, neither among all that walks the all-bountiful mother earth, nor all that journeys on wings through the wide air, nor all that cuts the wild waves in the deep; so upon those conspicuous birds there gleams fire blended with purpling gold, ablaze. I will not tell of the chilling race of the jagged hedgehog, the smaller kind; for to the sharp-haired hedgehogs belong twin grievous forms and a chilling encircling fence; for some are small and worthless, bristling with little jutting spines; but others are far greater in size, and on either side bristle sharp with stronger points. I leave the threefold breeds, the evil likeness, of apes; for who would not loathe such a race, shameful to behold, feeble, hateful, hard to look upon, of shifting counsel? They, having borne two ill-shaped dear children, do not divide their love equally between the two, but love the one and hate the other in their wrath; and in the very arms of their parents the loved one dies. Nor indeed do the songs wish to sing of the earth-born tribes of moles, grass-eating and blind, even if an unbelievable rumour has crossed to men that the moles boast descent from the blood of king Phineus, whom the famous Thracian hill reared; for once Phaethon the Titan was angry with Phineus, wroth over the victory of prophetic Phoebus, and robbed him of his light, and sent the shameless tribes, the Harpies, winged, bitter, hearth-haunting breeds. But when, journeying after the golden prize on the Argo, toiling with Jason, the two famous sons of Boreas, Zetes and Calais, pitied the old man and then slew those tribes, and gave sweet food to his wretched mouth. Yet not even so did Phaethon lull his anger, but at once he made him a race of moles that were not before; therefore now it remains blind and ravenous in its feeding.

But now that we have sung the tribes of horned beasts, bulls and deer and the splendid broad-horned ones, and gazelles and oryxes and the gleaming iorci, and all others on whose heads is armour above, come now, goddess, let us tell of the jagged-toothed company of flesh-eating beasts and the tusked breeds. And first to the lion let us dedicate the famous strain. The Curetes were the nurses of Zeus, the overpowering son of Cronus, when he was newly born, and Rhea, who stole the child away from his pitiless father Cronus, laid him in the bosom of Crete. But the son of Heaven, seeing the strong new-suckling boy, first changed the splendid guardians of Zeus and made them beasts, transforming the Curetes. And they, since by the counsels of the god a human form they had cast off, Cronus's gift, and clothed themselves as lions, afterward, by the gifts of Zeus, hold great sway over the mountain-haunting beasts, and the dread swift car of Rhea, blessed in childbirth, they draw beneath the yoke. Varied are the tribes and the forms among these beasts, each kind apart. Those that, by the outpourings of the loud-roaring river, by the wide-flowing Tiris, the archer land of Armenia bore, and the much-sowing, well-pastured land of the Parthians, are yellow-haired and not so strong. A thicker neck they bear, and a great head, gleaming eyes and brows high and deep, ample, drooping over the nose; and from the neck and from the jaws on either side swift manes wave thick. Those again the great-gifted soil of the Erembi rears, which the tribes of men call blessed; these too have necks and shaggy chests, and from their eyes flash gleams of fire, and they are conspicuous beyond all others; but the boundless earth has got a small breed of these. A great throng in deep-clodded, thirsty Libya roars and rumbles, the roaring of mighty lions, no longer shaggy, and a faint gleam runs over them; terrible in face and neck; and over all their limbs they bear faintly the dark flower of cyanus, soiled; boundless is the strength in their limbs, and over the kingly lions the Libyan lions hold great sway. And once from the Ethiopians there came over to the Libyan land, a great marvel to behold, a black-skinned, fair-maned lion, broad above in the head, hairy of foot, fiery of eye, reddened only at the yellow mouth. I saw, I did not learn by hearsay, that bloody beast, and it came as an envoy to kingly eyes. The tribes of lions do not crave food all their days, but the one cares for feasting, the other again for toil; nor do they take their sleep in the innermost corners of a rock, but openly they sleep, rolling a bold-hearted spirit, and slumber wherever the towering evening night overtakes them. I heard this too from the lion-keeping men, that the tawny lion bears beneath its right paw a swift numbness, with which it bends all the knees of beasts. Five times the female loosens her girdle for offspring; the report is truly idle, that she bears but one. Five she bears first; then four she travails of cubs; and next in order below, from the third womb three came forth; from the fourth twin children; and last the mother bore one, from the womb that bears the best, the famous king, the lion. The deadly leopards are a twofold race; some are larger to look upon and thicker in the broad back, and others are smaller, but in spirit no whit inferior; the forms of both are wrought alike, save only the tail, which is the other way to behold; in the smaller it is the larger, in the large the smaller. Well-knit are the thighs, the body long, the eye bright; the pupils gleam grey-glancing beneath the lids, grey-glancing at once and red within, like things on fire, blazing; but beneath the teeth about the mouth are pale and venomous. The hide is dappled, and over the all-shining colour it is dusky, with thick-set darkening spots. Most swiftly it runs, and bravely charges straight; you would say, when you saw it, it was borne through the air. And this tribe too the singers proclaim to have been of old the nurses of grape-bearing Bacchus; therefore even now they greatly rejoice in wine, receiving in their mouths the great gift of Dionysus. What cause from men changed the famous women into this savage race of leopards, I shall sing again. Yes, and you may behold another swift twofold race, the conspicuous lynxes; for some are to see small, and arm themselves against the smaller hares; others again are larger, and leap easily upon fair-horned deer and the sharper oryxes. In form both have clothed themselves quite alike; equal beneath the lids are the gleams from their eyes that flash lovely; the faces of both are bright, the head small, the ear curved; only the colour is unlike to behold; over the smaller lynxes runs a reddish hide, over the larger a saffron and brimstone-like bloom. Above all these tribes are amazed at their own offspring, the bright-eyed lynxes and the fiery-eyed lions, the deadly leopards and the windswift tigers. And when their new-suckling cubs in the thickets fearless hunters secretly carry off, and they afterward, returning back, behold suddenly the empty homes and the deserted dwellings, they wail shrilly an endless lament, and from afar they send forth a much-groaning cry, just as when, the homeland sacked by the spear and burning with fierce fire, the women, flung about their children, weep greatly. So great a love of offspring and of new-born young did the god instil in the heart; not in men alone, who devise all things by their minds, but also in serpents and fishes and even in the ravening beasts and the high-soaring flocks of birds; so much is nature stronger than all else. What care of offspring in the waves the dolphin ever has, and the grey shark and the ill-blowing seal! How among birds an unceasing longing they have for their young, the vultures and the deep-voiced doves and the eagle tribes and the long-lived crows! How a hen in the house, sharing the hearth with men, newly delivered, frisking about her young chicks, when she sees a hawk swooping down over the roof, shrieks sharply at once and starts up with a sharp cry, and lifts her neck high, arching it to the air, and on either side quickly bristles all her feathers, and lets all her wings sink to the ground; and the timid chicks, foot-soldiers, twitter beneath the winged wall; but she both routs and drives off the shameless bird, guarding her dear children, which she still feeds while small, wingless, loosed from the bonds of the birth-loosing chambers. So too among beasts the loud-roaring lionesses and the swift leopards and the dapple-backed tigers stand before their young and fight with the hunters, and for their own offspring they endure to be slain, setting themselves against the spearmen, against men; nor ever do they shudder, in the contest for their race, not at the oncoming throng of javelin-hurling men, not at the gleaming bronze and the flashing iron, nor at the swift casts of darts and the thick-flung stones, but they strive either to die first or to save their young. The wild bears, a murderous race, of shifting counsel, have clothed themselves in thick, hard-to-handle fur, and a form not gentle, with utterly mirthless faces; a jagged, deadly, long mouth, a dark-blue nose, a swift eye, a swift ankle, a keen body, a broad head, hands like the hands of mortals, and feet again like feet, a terrible roar, a treacherous heart, a savage spirit, and much Cythera, going beyond all measure; for day and night, longing for love, the females themselves rush eagerly upon the males, seldom leaving the all-delightful marriage-bed, conceiving young when they swell in the womb. For it is not the law among beasts, when the belly is full, for those going to the bed to perform the work of love, save only for the lynxes and the feeble hares. But the bear, longing for love and loathing to keep the bed widowed for her young, has dared to devise this: before the hour of birth comes, before the appointed day, she presses out her womb and forces the birth-goddesses. So great is her lust, so great her race toward Aphrodite. She bears young half-finished and without limbs, flesh without mark, jointless, formless to behold, and her care is for both love and the rearing of children; new-delivered though she still is, at once she beds with the male. She licks with her tongue her dear offspring, just as calves lick one another with their tongues by turns, delighting in each other; and the fair-horned ox is gladdened by the ox's skin; nor do they wander apart, until they have shed sweet desire; and they cheer the heart of the herdsman following them. So the bear, licking, moulds her dear children, until with their whimperings they mutter shamelessly. Yes, and above all she fears the wintry onset, shaggy though she is; and when snow powders everything, the western wind scattering it thick over all, she hides in a cave, where she may find sufficient shelter, and, lacking food, she licks her feet and hands, as if being milked, and so steals away the urging of her belly. Such things, I suppose, in the depths of the wide-wayed sea the crooked octopuses devise beside the waves, which in midwinter, dreading the chilling threat, hide in the flat rocks, eating their own tentacles; but when the wet, well-nourishing spring blooms, swiftly the new shoots grow for them again, and once more, fair-tressed, they swim the long sea. Next let us tell of the well-ankled, dusky, swift, storm-footed, strong-hoofed, lofty wild ass; the eye is bright, the body sufficient, broad to behold, silvery in colour, long-eared, swiftest to run; a black stripe runs about the middle of its spine, ringed on either side with snowy crowns. It eats fodder; the grass-feeding earth feeds it abundantly, but it itself is good food for strong beasts. The storm-footed tribes of wild asses, wholly jealous, glory in their many mates, and pride themselves; the females follow where their mate leads; to pasture they make their way, when he chooses to bid them, to the springs of rivers, the wine of beasts, and again straightway to the shaggy homes, when evening brings sleep. Jealousy in all the males against their own infant sons a wholly savage, shameless frenzy stirs; for when the female has the labour of childbirth, he sits very near and watches his own offspring face on; and when the babe falls beside the mother's feet, if it is female, he loves the child, and on either side licking with his tongue he cherishes his dear offspring; but if he sees it is male, then, then indeed he stirs his heart, the beast raging at the mother with baleful jealousy; and he leaps forth, eager to cut off with his jaws the young one's manhood, lest afterward the new race should grow up. But she, though new-delivered and weak from the birth, as a mother defends her wretched child under attack. And as when in much-grieving war, before its mother's eyes, pitiless spearmen slay the infant, and again drag the mother herself, while it still gasps in death, twined about her son, wailing a great mournful cry, tearing her soft cheek, and below her breasts drenched with warm blood and lukewarm milk; so too the female wild ass over her son seems wholly to make a piteous moaning and to wail her ill fortune. You would say that the wretched one, bestriding her own child, spoke gentle words and uttered a pleading speech: "Husband, husband, why now are your features made harsh, and your eyes reddened, that before were gleaming? Do you not see before you the brow of stone-working Medusa, not the venom-eating brood of the pitiless dragoness, not the all-lawless cub of the mountain-roaming lioness? The child whom I bore in misery, whom we prayed for to the gods, your own child—will you with your jaws make him no male? Hold, my love, do not cut; why have you cut me? what have you done? You have made the child nothing, blinding his whole body. Wretched am I, all luckless in this most untimely birth, and you, child, all wretched in your most sinful sire. Wretched am I, thrice unhappy, who travailed an empty birth, and you, child, cut not by the claws of lions, but by the hateful lion-jaws of a sire." Such things, one would say, the all-luckless mother speaks about her infant child; and he, caring nothing, with bloody mouth feasts on the joyless food of his child. Father Zeus, how wholly savage is the heart of jealousy! That beast, mightier than nature to behold you made, lord, and gave it the sharp rush of fire, and granted it to bear an adamantine blade in its right hand. It did not spare dear children for their sweet parents, nor, when it comes, does it know comrades and kinsmen, nor blood-kin, whenever it meets, grievous and boundless. That beast too of old armed against their own children the very demigods and the blameless demigoddesses, the son of Aegeus, Theseus, and the son of Aeolus, Athamas, the Attic woman and Procne and Thracian Philomela and Colchian Medea and conspicuous Themisto. But nevertheless, after the race of grievous mortals, it set before the beasts the deadly Thyestean table. There is on the well-cliffed borders of the Ethiopians a great tribe of wild horses, armed with venomous double tusks; and of their feet not a single hoof, but they bear a double cloven hoof, like deer; the neck-mane, bestriding the middle of the spine, runs back to the very tail; nor ever did the dread overweening race endure the slavery of mortals; but even if at some time the black-skinned Indians should take the wild horse with well-twisted nooses in their crafty ambushes, it will neither taste food at once with its lips nor drink, but the deadly creature is ready to die rather than bear the slavish yoke. Mark also two foe-meeting, jagged-toothed tribes, the sheep-slaying wolf and again the hard-to-look-on hyena, the one the destroyer of flocks and goatfolds, the other hateful to whelps and the braver hounds; the one the nightly, inescapable raider of the belly, the wily snatcher of lambs and kids, the other being a night-rover and a night-wanderer, because for her by night is light, and again darkness after dawn. The forms of both these bloody beasts are unlike; for the one you may see all like to the larger shepherd hounds, and a shaggy tail follows; but the other arches the middle of her spine, and all about is shaggy, and her dread body is inscribed with dark stripes thick-set on either side; narrow and long is she in back and tail; and the singers proclaim the hides of both to be chilling; if you cut the hyena's and wear it about your feet, you would wear a great terror to mighty hounds, and the dogs, when you tread in such sandals, do not bark at you in return, though before they were barking. And if you flay a wolf and fashion from its hide a sweet-sounding Didymaean drum, a fruit-destroying drum, alone among all it has rung a deep-booming sound and alone it clatters, and the drums that before were tuneful it silences and deafens every voice. For even dead the sheep shudder at the dead wolf. A marvel too I have heard about the dappled hyenas, that male and female change with the year, and now one becomes the hard-to-look-on bridegroom, ceaselessly longing for love, and then again is seen as a female bride in travail and a careful mother. But there are five grey-haired races of wolves, and their forms men have marked as unlike one another, the shepherd men, to whom they are most hostile. First, the one they call the bold-hearted archer; tawny in all its form, but with rounded limbs, and it bears a head much larger and swift legs; its belly is whitened with grey spots; terribly it howls and leaps quite on high, ever shaking its head and glaring fire. Another is greater in size, but again long of limb, swifter than all the wolves; men call it the hawk and the snatcher. With much whirring it goes very early to the hunt, at the first twilight; for easily it lacks food; a silvery hue gleams on its flanks and tail, and it dwells in the great mountains; but when, in the winter season, the chilling snow, poured from the clouds, has covered them, then the deadly-minded beast comes near the city too, clothed in all shamelessness for the sake of food, and it draws near secretly and very quietly, until it presses upon its prey; and at once with its swift claws it seizes it. There is one that, over the snow-stricken peaks of Taurus, haunting the Cilician heights and the headlands of Amanus, is fair to see, pre-eminent among beasts, which they call the golden one, flashing with abundant fleece, no wolf, but a beast far surpassing the wolf, most lofty, whetted with bronze lips, boundless in strength. Often the unwearied bronze, often the stone it has steadily pierced, and the pointed iron. And it knows the Dog-star and fears it when it rises; at once it sinks into a cleft of the wide earth or into a lightless cave, until the sun and the star of the deadly Dog cease from their parching heat. Two are the Acmones, a murderous race, small in the neck, broadest in the back, but shaggy-haired in the thighs and feet and face, smaller, small in the eyes. Of these the one with silvery back and white belly shines all over, and is dark only at the very tips of its paws; some men have called it the grey-haired kite. But the other appears with darkening colours, smaller than the former, but in strength not inferior. It hunts terribly, charging at the hares; and all the hairs over its limbs bristle upright. And often wolves have approached the bloody leopards for the bed, whence comes a strong-hearted race, the jackals; together they bear a double soiled bloom, the mother in the hide, and the father again in the face. Next let us sing the famous body of the tiger, than which cunning nature has given nothing more delightful for the eyes to behold among the great company of beasts. So far does the tiger surpass among beasts as the fair peacock among the birds of the air. You would think it altogether a mountain lioness, save only for the hide, with which it is ringed, dappled, gleaming intricate and shining with flowers. Such a fiery flash beneath the lids its eyes dart; and the body is of such a kind, strong, well-fleshed; such the long-shadowing tail; such the face about the mouth; such above the brow droops; such the gleaming teeth. It is swifter than the swiftest, pre-eminent among beasts; for it is like to Zephyr itself, its father, in running; yet not its father; who could believe these things, that beasts should be subdued by a wind as bridegroom? For that is an empty tale, that this tribe is all female and bedless of any male; for often you might see a many-flowered fair mate; yet easily you could not take it; for, leaving its young, it steadily flees, when it sees the hunters; but the mother, following her cubs and grieving in spirit, a great joy to hunters, comes straight to the nets. The boar, far pre-eminent among the warlike beasts, loves its couches in the inmost depths of the cliffs, and above all it loathes the much-echoing din of beasts. Restlessly it wanders, rushing upon the female, and, mad with love, it swells; upright on its neck bristle the hairs, like the crests of high-plumed helmets, and it lets fall foam upon the ground; and the fence of its teeth clatters white with hot panting; and there is more wrath about its loves than shame. But if the female, cowering, awaits it, it quenches all its wrath and lulls the beast's onset; but if, refusing, she flees the loving bed, at once, stirred by the hot fiery gadfly, either it accomplishes the union by force, mastering her by might, or it lays her dead in the dust, charging with its jaws. There is a report about the boar, that within its white tusk it secretly holds a fierce fiery heat.
